title: Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions
one_liner: Track carriers' filed AI exclusions and tell brokers, 90 days before renewal, which clients just lost AI coverage, then place the affirmative buy-back.
customer: Independent agencies and regional brokers (10-200 staff) with commercial books, their E&O carriers, and MGAs.
problem: Since January 2026 ISO-style generative-AI endorsements (CG 40 47 and CG 40 48) and far broader carrier forms, such as W. R. Berkley's 'absolute' AI exclusion, are attached at renewal, often buried. Clients use AI in ways they never disclosed. Brokers carry E&O exposure for failing to warn, and no tool maps which of a broker's 300 clients face AI exclusions or what AI each client actually uses.
solution: A rate and form filing scraper (public SERFF filing access) plus an endorsement parser that normalises exclusion breadth: gen-AI only versus any AI, bodily injury versus advertising injury, vendor-supplied AI. It feeds a renewal calendar imported from agency-management CSVs. A 12-question client AI-use questionnaire, optionally backed by an SSO or expense-report scan for AI tools. Output is a one-page 'AI coverage gap letter' plus a list of affirmative AI markets for placement.
why_now: 1 Jan 2027 renewals are the first big cycle after the Verisk endorsements became available, and AIG, Great American and Berkley filings landed through 2026. Affirmative AI capacity now exists (Armilla via Lloyd's, AIUC, Munich Re aiSure), so a gap and its fix can be sold together.
revenue_model: $250-800 per month per agency, $150-600 per gap letter for non-subscribers, 10-15% commission on affirmative cover placed, and $2-5k per month filing-intelligence subscriptions for MGAs and carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is triggered by their own E&O fear, not curiosity about AI. The filings are public but unreadable, so the moat is a normalised exclusion database nobody at a brokerage has time to build. Silent AI cuts both ways: an unexcluded policy is a reason to ask for affirmative cover, so the gap letter also works as a sales tool for the broker.
first_30_days: Scrape SERFF filings in five large states and build the tracker. Start a free weekly 'AI exclusion tracker' newsletter aimed at 500 brokers. Offer 10 agencies a $500 concierge gap audit on their five biggest accounts. Sign one affirmative-AI MGA for placement referrals.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Patra (AI Policy Checking), Quandri, Zywave Apex / Advisor Agent, Testudo. White space: A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. Pieces exist separately. Patra reads commercial policies for hidden exclusions but is not AI-specific. Quandri and Zywave own the 90-day renewal trigger but show no exclusion-level AI flagging. Testudo and Armilla offer AI-use mapping and placement but only for their own paper.

Three parts of the plan are weak. (a) The SERFF scraper and exclusion database are not a moat. Trades Coverage already compiled 4,078 records for free. Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs and ShadowLock publish free trackers, and Certian even ships CC BY 4.0 CSV and JSON. (b) A filing shows a carrier adopted a form in a state. It does not show the form is attached to client X's policy, so the real signal is the policy document, not the filing. (c) SERFF filing access covers admitted markets only. Surplus lines is where most E&O, D&O and tech-E&O AI exclusions sit, and it is largely invisible to SERFF.

Wedge that looks unserved: commercial professional-liability and tech-E&O accounts (design firms, law, accounting, software, agencies) where exclusions are broadest and most bespoke, for independent agencies without an in-house risk-advisory team, priced as a renewal-review add-on rather than a filings database.

title: Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard
one_liner: Publish and run the defensible smoke, ash and soot assessment protocol that California insurers, adjusters and lawyers will need on January 1, 2027, because the official technical standard will not exist until 2028-2029.
customer: California carriers, the FAIR Plan and their TPAs (for AB 1795's 30-day inspection and testing obligations), plus public adjusters, policyholder attorneys, and escrow, lender and buyer parties in standing-home sales. Homeowners pay via their insurer, PA or directly.
problem: California signed AB 1795 and AB 1642 on Sept 15, 2026. From Jan 1, 2027, insurers must inspect within 30 days, pay for necessary testing, keep paying ALE until restoration, and face a presumption that ash, soot and char in a standing home are fire-caused. But the state toxics department will not finish lead and asbestos standards until end of 2028 and other contaminant standards until 2029. Meanwhile tens of thousands of claims will need a protocol that survives litigation; existing vendor assessments are already accused of being substandard, and capacity of qualified industrial hygienists is scarce and expensive.
solution: An independent, openly published interim assessment protocol built on existing standards (IICRC S700, established sampling and lab methods, EPA/HUD dust-wipe criteria), developed with certified industrial hygienists and a toxicologist. Delivered as a product: a sampling-plan generator (which rooms, surfaces and ducts, how many samples), a trained technician network with kits and a chain-of-custody app, remote IH sign-off, a lab partner, a compliance-clock dashboard for carriers, and a 'smoke clearance certificate' for resale and escrow. Priced at a fraction of full CIH scopes.
why_now: The laws were signed two weeks ago with an effective date of Jan 1, 2027, LA County is investigating Farmers over Eaton/Palisades claim denials, a proposed class action targets vendor assessments, and carriers oppose but must comply. The gap between the compliance date and the state standard is a 2-3 year window in which the best-documented protocol becomes the de facto reference, and other fire states (Colorado, Oregon, Hawaii) are watching.
revenue_model: Per-home assessment of $1,800-$4,500 (paid by insurer under AB 1795 or the policyholder), $500 clearance-certificate add-on, lab pass-through margin, SaaS compliance dashboard for carriers at $2-$5 per claim per month, and training and certification fees for restoration technicians.
non_obvious_insight: In smoke disputes the lab is rarely the fight; the fight is the sampling design and the pass/fail threshold. Carriers whose vendors sample five spots and compare against urban background dust get 'clean' results by construction. Whoever publishes a transparent, replicable sampling grid with chain of custody writes the eventual standard, because regulators borrow the protocol with the most field data.
first_30_days: Recruit two CIHs and one toxicologist as an advisory board and draft 'Interim Smoke Assessment Protocol v0.1' for public comment. Train 6-10 IICRC-certified restoration technicians and buy sampling kits. Sell 20 pilot assessments in Altadena and Palisades at a subsidized $950 through public adjusters and attorneys, gathering data and case studies. Pitch 3 carriers and 2 TPAs on 30-day compliance capacity before January 1, offering a pilot at cost in exchange for using the protocol.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven.

title: AI Chat-History Exposure Assessments for Breach Counsel
one_liner: When infostealers grab employees' AI sessions, tell breach counsel what the attacker could actually have read and whether notification is triggered.
customer: Incident-response boutiques, privacy and breach law firms, cyber-insurer panel vendors, and enterprise DPOs. Priced per incident.
problem: Infostealer logs exposed AI sessions tied to 80,000+ corporate domains, and 358 of 482 large companies analyzed had stolen ChatGPT/OpenAI sessions. A stolen session is a searchable archive of contracts, source code, and personal data, and it bypasses MFA. IR tooling was built for mailboxes and file shares, so nobody can say whether an AI-history breach triggers legal notification.
solution: Ingest infostealer-feed hits mapped to employee AI accounts. Combine them with the customer's enterprise export or compliance-API data to classify the sampled chats after the theft window by data class (PII, PHI, credentials, deal information, source code). Deliver a notification-decision memo, an affected-person list, remediation steps (session revocation, key rotation), and an insurer-ready timeline.
why_now: The 2026 infostealer data shows stolen AI sessions at scale. Enterprise AI adoption now puts sensitive work in chat, and insurers are adding AI exclusions, so they want scoping evidence before paying.
revenue_model: $5-25K per incident, with $1-2K per month monitoring retainers and channel referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The breach is not the stolen cookie but the content behind it, and notification law turns on data, not credentials. No tool in the IR stack handles AI transcripts, so a small team can own the category before platform vendors bother.
first_30_days: Sign 3 IR boutiques as channel partners. Build a classification pipeline over enterprise chat exports. Run the first paid assessments at a $7.5K flat fee using hits from commercial infostealer-intel feeds.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hudson Rock (Cavalier, infostealers.com, CavalierGPT), SpyCloud, Flare, Constella Intelligence. White space: Across the pages I could fetch, no vendor sells the specific deliverable: a counsel-facing 'what could the attacker have read, and does notification trigger' determination for a stolen AI session. The gap sits between three groups. Infostealer-intel vendors (Hudson Rock, SpyCloud, Flare, Constella) detect the stolen session but stop there. AI-DLP and DSPM vendors (Varonis, Cyera, Harmonic, Cyberhaven, Reco, Purview) classify current or real-time chat data for the customer's own governance. Breach-review platforms (Relativity and IR firms) build notification lists but show no ingestion of AI chat transcripts. What remains open is the forensic and legal bridge: joining the theft window from the feed with provider-side session-access evidence and the chat content, then producing a privilege-friendly memo and affected-person list.

Caveats on the wedge:
- The WebSearch budget ran out, so I could not check funded startups, Product Hunt, YC or open-source projects. A stealth startup is possible.
- I could not verify the '358 of 482' or '80,000 domains' figures.
- The wedge depends on data access. A theft of a personal or free-tier account leaves the employer with no export. Only Enterprise and Edu tenants have admin export or Compliance API data, and I could not confirm the current API terms because the OpenAI help pages returned 403.
- A stolen cookie in a feed does not prove the attacker viewed the chats, so the assessment depends on provider audit logs that only OpenAI or the tenant admin can see.
- Any vendor holding the customer's chat data (Cyera, Varonis, Purview) can add this as a services line quickly.

title: Vacant-Unit Meter Watchdog and Insurance Vacancy Log
one_liner: Uses utility smart-meter data that owners already have rights to, so PMs can catch squatters, leaks and freeze risk in empty units within hours, without installing any hardware.
customer: Property managers and owners of single-family and 2-to-20-unit portfolios (100 to 2,000 doors). They already pay the utilities on vacant units and carry standard dwelling or small-building policies with a vacancy clause. Buyer is the PM's ops director or the owner. Secondary buyers later are E&S and landlord-program insurers.
problem: When a unit is occupied, the tenant is the sensor and tells you about leaks. When it is vacant you are blind for 20 to 60 days. Water damage, squatters, stolen copper, AC left running and burst pipes all happen in that window. Most property policies restrict vandalism, water damage and theft after roughly 60 days of vacancy, and the claim gets denied or cut exactly when the loss is biggest. Squatter removal is also time-critical: in many states an intruder found on day 2 is a police trespass matter, while the same person on day 30 needs a months-long court eviction. Walk-throughs are weekly at best, and the maintenance tech skips them when busy.
solution: Vacancy Vitals connects to interval electric and water data through owner-authorized utility APIs (Green Button Connect, or aggregators like UtilityAPI). The owner's account is usually the one active during vacancy, so no tenant consent is needed. Rules fire on patterns: continuous 24/7 water flow (leak), electric baseline above the empty-unit norm (someone living there, a crypto miner, a grow), a heating or cooling setpoint far outside range (pipe-freeze or mold risk), and a sudden drop to zero in a unit that should be running HVAC. Alerts go by text to the on-call tech with a one-tap 'send someone' button. The product also generates a time-stamped weekly vacancy-inspection log (data check plus a tech photo check-in) formatted for carriers' vacancy-permit or inspection conditions. That log is what preserves coverage.
why_now: Anti-squatter laws were passed in a wave in 2024 and 2025 (for example Florida and Georgia), which makes early detection more valuable. Smart-meter penetration passed roughly 70% of US electric customers. Insurers have been tightening on water-damage and vacancy exposure for several years. AI-based anomaly detection on interval data is now cheap. (Current state-by-state anti-squatter rules and utility API coverage should be verified before launch.)
revenue_model: $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month on usage, or a flat $1 to $2 per door per month portfolio subscription. Later, insurer-paid or insurer-discounted programs: the carrier pays a fee per monitored door in exchange for lower loss ratios and a vacancy-clause waiver.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest sensor for a vacant house is the meter the utility already installed, and the account is in the owner's name during vacancy. Nobody in proptech treats owner-account utility data as a security and insurance-compliance feed. They sell $60 leak sensors and cameras instead. The other secret is legal timing. The value is not detecting the squatter, it is detecting them in the first 48 hours, when the law treats it as trespass rather than a tenancy.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 to 5 SFR or small-multifamily PMs, offer a free 'backtest', and pull 12 months of interval data for units that were vacant. Show them the incidents the tool would have caught. These are usually a few leaks, a few unauthorized occupants and several HVAC-left-on units, each worth $1,000 to $15,000. Build a UtilityAPI-based prototype with three rules, text alerts and a weekly PDF log. Charge $99 per month per portfolio during the pilot, then convert to per-unit pricing. In parallel, talk to two independent insurance agents who write landlord programs, to learn the exact vacancy-permit language and to get a warm intro for the carrier channel.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Arcadia (utility data platform), UtilityAPI, Wint Water Intelligence, SmartRent. White space: I found no product that does what this idea proposes: rules on owner-authorized utility interval data to detect squatters, unauthorized occupancy, leaks and HVAC problems in vacant units, then produce a carrier-formatted vacancy-inspection log with no installed hardware. The alternatives are hardware (Wint, SmartRent, Minut, Flume), utility data plumbing (Arcadia, UtilityAPI), or bill-management tools (Conservice, EnergyCAP). None of their pages pitch vacant-unit security or insurance vacancy compliance. Three things are genuinely unserved: (1) electric-baseline occupancy detection in a vacant unit, which the water-focused players cannot do; (2) an inspection log formatted for carrier vacancy-permit conditions; (3) small portfolios of 100 to 2,000 doors, which Wint and SmartRent do not serve well. I could not find how commonly PMs use utility-supplied continuous-flow leak alerts (water utilities with AMI portals, my background knowledge, unverified). Research limits: the WebSearch budget was used up, so no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches were possible. The verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and background knowledge, and the absence of a direct competitor is not proven. Main risks: (a) UtilityAPI lists $2.40 to $30 per meter per month for scheduled monitoring, so on a $1 to $2 per door or $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month price, data cost could exceed revenue unless you use free Green Button Connect direct integrations or price higher; (b) interval water data through third-party APIs is thin, because most water utilities have no Green Button Connect, and leaks are the biggest loss, so the water rule may only work in a few metros; (c) each owner must authorize each utility account, a real onboarding cost at 100 to 2,000 doors; (d) I found nothing showing carriers accept a monitoring log in place of a vacancy permit or endorsement, so the 'log preserves coverage' claim is unproven; (e) the '48-hour trespass window' insight is unverified. The Florida HB 621 page I fetched confirms sheriff removal and a July 1, 2024 effective date but gives no time threshold, and Wikipedia confirms Alabama's 2024 24-hour removal law, so statute-specific timing needs a lawyer.

title: Town-Paid Private Road Census and Formation Bounty
one_liner: Sell New England towns (and their municipal insurance pools) a four-week census of every private road's legal status and emergency-access risk, then earn a per-road bounty for each neighbor group converted into a recorded association with a named point of contact.
customer: Town managers, road commissioners and fire chiefs of small and mid-sized Maine towns (2,000-15,000 residents), then NH and VT. Multi-town buyers: regional councils and planning commissions, and municipal risk pools that fund loss-control services for member towns (Maine Municipal Association's risk program, NH Primex, Vermont VLCT PACIF, all from prior knowledge and unverified here). Secondary payers: developers, via a road-association setup line on the town's subdivision application fee. Residents co-pay a small share.
problem: Every town has dozens to hundreds of private ways with unknown legal status. The town usually cannot spend public money on them (varies by state, to be confirmed per state), yet it is blamed when an ambulance or plow cannot pass a failed culvert, when a subdivision road approved on the condition that a road association be formed decays years later, or when residents petition the town to accept a broken road that would cost six figures to rebuild to town standard. After a storm, state aid wants an organized counterparty. NC's post-Helene private-road program (verified) required a single point of contact and proof of ownership, plus a 50% cost share. The town has no inventory to hand over. Neighbors are stuck in a collective-action deadlock, because nobody wants to be the one who calls the meeting.
solution: Step 1, a fixed-price Private Road Census, roughly $6,500 per town. We ingest parcel GIS, E911 road-name files, registry-of-deeds documents and any culvert or bridge inventory the town has. Language models read the recorded instruments to flag whether a maintenance agreement exists and what it says. For each private way we output parcels served, recorded instrument yes/no, whether an active association exists, contact if any, single-access and stream-crossing flags, and a fire-truck-passability risk score reviewed with the fire chief. The town gets a ranked list, map and memo. Step 2, activation. The town mails a letter on its own letterhead to the top 40 roads with a pre-filled petition for the statutory meeting. In Maine a few owners can petition a notary, and the town letter breaks the who-goes-first deadlock. We run the meetings, and an attorney-supervised covenant is recorded. The town pays a $600 bounty for each completed association (recorded instrument plus officers and point of contact), and residents co-pay about $500. Step 3, a registry subscription at about $2,400 per town per year. It keeps contacts, insurance certificates, reserve attestations and condition photos current, and yields a disaster-ready roads list for the state emergency agency after a storm. Step 4, the town adds a setup fee to subdivision applications so new roads get an association and reserve schedule at approval.
why_now: The cost stack collapsed. Reading recorded instruments for 120 roads used to mean about 120 title searches at hundreds of dollars each. With document extraction plus human QA it is roughly a tenth of that, which is what makes a fixed-price census possible. Storm events keep exposing the same gap, and NC's $175M program (verified) shows states will pay for repair but only through an organized counterparty. Parcel GIS and E911 layers are now open in most New England states. Municipal risk pools are always looking for loss-control programs to justify member subsidies (hypothesis to test). The disaster-aid windows (NC applications closed Feb 2026) show that the next program will again favor roads that are already organized.
revenue_model: Census $6,500 per town, or a regional-council package of 10-12 towns at about $55-65k. Formation bounty $600 per association from the town, plus a $500 resident co-pay, or about $1,100 per road. Registry $2,400 per town per year. Developer setup fee about $1,200 per new subdivision, collected through the town. A town with 120 private ways where 60% are informal has about 70 candidates. If 40% convert in year 1, that is 28 roads, about $31k in bounties and co-pays, plus census and registry, or about $40k per town in year 1. 25 towns would be about $1M. Conversion rate is the key hypothesis. Risk pools could subsidize the census for members, making the insurer a second payer.
non_obvious_insight: The town is not buying road repairs or software. It is buying a legal counterparty for roads it cannot touch, plus a defensible record that it knew about the risk and acted. That is liability hygiene, an easier budget line than subsidizing private roads. The official letter is the cheapest neighbor-activation channel that exists, because it dissolves the who-goes-first deadlock that makes formation so slow closing-by-closing. One buyer delivers dozens of roads, which inverts the parent's per-road CAC. The census data, once assembled across towns, becomes a state-level inventory that emergency agencies, lenders and title underwriters would pay for.
first_30_days: Pick one pilot town with open parcel GIS and online registry access, ideally a lakes-region Maine town of about 4,000 people. Build a free 30-road slice of the census in 10 days from public data. Walk it to the road commissioner, fire chief and town manager, and ask them for the 5 roads they fear most. Ask to mail an official letter to 10 pilot roads and run 2 statutory meetings within 30 days. In parallel, call 3 regional councils and the risk-management teams of the Maine, NH and Vermont municipal associations to test whether they would subsidize census work as loss control. Target one signed $4,500 first-town census (typically under small-purchase thresholds, to be confirmed) and one pilot association recorded. Riskiest assumptions: town willingness to pay a per-road bounty, and letter-to-meeting conversion above 25%.
lineage: mutation of I0048 ('Private Road Associations in a Box'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:
- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest. | How this version avoids them: PayHOA and the mainstream HOA platforms: they sell to associations and managers, never to towns, and require an existing association. We create the association, and dues admin stays a thin link to whatever tool the road picks. DIY templates and local attorneys: they serve a single closing, and we are town-sponsored and mass-produced with attorney supervision behind it, so we are a customer of their legal review rather than a rival. State statutes and county road districts: we operationalize the statute at scale for towns rather than asking residents to self-serve. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: a demand proof and a template for who will need our pre-qualified registry after the next storm. Local road-association managers (unidentified): potential subcontractors for annual administration, not competitors for a town-level census. Town asset-management and GIS vendors such as Cartegraph or OpenGov (from prior knowledge, unverified): they track public roads and would not create legal counterparties on private ones.

title: China-Asset Diligence Desk for Pharma BD
one_liner: A bilingual scientist-plus-software sprint that verifies China-sourced drug packages (raw data, GLP and CMC standing, ownership chain) in 72 hours for US buyers.
customer: Pharma BD&L teams, NewCo-building VCs, royalty funds and mid-cap biotechs in-licensing Chinese assets.
problem: About one-third of 2025 licensing spend involved China-sourced drugs (Jefferies) and the pace accelerated in 2026 (Lilly-InnoCare up to $3.35B, Merck-SciBrunch $2.1B). Diligence infrastructure looks thin (inference): data packages are in Chinese formats, raw-data and audit-trail norms differ, and CRO and CDMO GLP or GMP standing is hard to verify. BIOSECURE, enacted Dec 18, 2025, requires OMB to publish the list of biotechnology companies of concern by December 2026 and FAR rules follow, adding an ownership and supply-chain axis.
solution: A fixed-price 'Asset Verification Sprint'. LLM-assisted translation and structured extraction of study reports. Bilingual scientists spot-check raw data and audit trails. Verify CRO and CDMO inspection histories (NMPA, FDA, EMA) and check ownership chains against the BIOSECURE lists. Deliver a Western-format gap analysis for IND-enabling needs (GLP tox acceptability, CMC comparability).
why_now: Deal flow is at record levels, BIOSECURE list publication is due in about three months, and biopharma layoffs (15,000+) free bilingual ex-pharma scientists.
revenue_model: $25-70k per sprint, $150-300k annual retainers for NewCo-builder VCs, and supply-chain mapping as a second product once the BIOSECURE lists land.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is not legal or financial diligence. It is data literacy and tacit standards, for example what counts as GLP-grade raw data, and Western deal associates cannot read the packages. The same team and database serve a second product, supply-chain mapping, when the lists arrive.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-4 bilingual ex-pharma scientists. Price a $20k pilot sprint. Approach 5 NewCo VC platforms and 5 mid-size pharma BD heads. Build a CRO and CDMO inspection database from public regulator records.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Alacrita (biotech consulting network), Patsnap Synapse (AI drug asset due diligence reports), Pharmcube (Yaozhi / Pharma Insight consulting), Locust Walk / Banyan BioInnovations. White space: Nobody found sells what the idea specifies: a fixed-price, bilingual scientist-led verification of a China-sourced drug package's raw data and audit trails, GLP-tox acceptability for a US IND, CMC comparability, and CRO/CDMO standing, delivered as a Western-format gap memo for buyers with no China bench. Locust Walk's CEO says 'getting data out of the company can be challenging', and China's data-export and human-genetic-resources rules (Morgan Lewis playbook) may block raw-data transfer. title: Independent Big-Meter Audits With Refund Guarantee
one_liner: A brand-neutral audit of a utility's 100-400 largest meters: AMI history is turned into a ranked, field-tested list of under-registering accounts. It is sold as a fixed-price small purchase, refunded if verified annual recovery is under 2x the fee.
customer: Finance director or utility director at a combined water+sewer municipal utility with 10-40k connections. AMI (or monthly-read AMR) is fully deployed, there are 100-400 meters of 3 inch and larger, and there is no in-house crew to bench- or field-test large meters. A rate hearing or rate study is due within 9 months. Wedge accounts: hospitals, hotels, food and beverage plants, universities and laundries. These run all night on low flows, which is exactly where old compound and turbine meters under-read.
problem: The parent's ghost-parcel half is weak (permits trigger taps, ADUs are usually billed on a shared meter) and contingency contracts are restricted or slow in some states. Back-billing is legally capped and politically toxic. The real leak is quieter. The utility's most valuable meters are 15-30 years old and lose low-flow registration. The meter is also the instrument that would have to report its own failure. Every under-read gallon is lost twice, because sewer charges on commercial accounts are billed off the water read. Councils are approving 5-10% rate steps while nobody has tested the top-revenue meters. Meter vendors and distributors do test large meters, but their business is selling the replacement.
solution: Step 1: get one CSV of 24 months of reads or interval data for the top 100-400 accounts, plus the meter inventory (size, make, install year). Step 2: compute a 'low-flow fingerprint' per account: (a) share of hours with zero registered flow versus use-code and NAICS peers that show base load; (b) a hole in the flow histogram just below the compound-meter crossover or start-up flow; (c) step-downs after meter or endpoint changes; (d) zero-read or estimated-read streaks. Step 3: rank by expected annual dollars, water plus sewer. Step 4: an independent crew field-tests the top 12-15 (three flow rates, AWWA M6-style, in-situ rig) and issues test certificates. Step 5: deliver a council-ready 2-page brief ('this recovers $X a year and offsets Y points of the next rate step'), a brand-neutral replacement spec, and prospective-only correction as the default. Recovery comes from swapping the meter, not from back-billing. The measured under-registration also replaces the default assumption in the utility's AWWA/M36 water audit and raises its Data Validity Score.
why_now: Utilities that finished AMI in 2018-2022 now hold 4+ years of hourly data that no one has analyzed for revenue. PFAS, lead-line and pipe capex are forcing rate hikes into affordability fights, so 'prove we've fixed our own leaks first' is a strong council story. State water-audit mandates (for example Texas for systems with 3,300+ connections) create an annual moment when apparent losses are examined. Cheap data engineering means a two-person team can build the fingerprint model. Incumbent meter makers have no credible way to tell a customer that their installed base under-registers.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of about $24k (scan plus 12 independent tests), priced under typical small-purchase or informal-bid limits (to verify per state), refunded in full if verified annualized recoverable revenue is under 2x the fee. Add-ons: $1.5k per meter for post-swap verification; an annual 'Big Meter Monitor' at $8-15k a year per utility; licensing the screen to rate consultants and AMI vendors. An opt-in success share applies only in states where it is lawful, for ghost-parcel or sewer-only leads. Assumed unit economics: about $10k COGS per audit (about 30 analyst hours, 12 subcontracted tests at roughly $600-800). About 55-60% gross margin and about 30 audits a year for two people is roughly $700k, before monitor ARR.
non_obvious_insight: A refund guarantee on a fixed fee gets the benefits of contingency (zero risk, easy yes) without the parts that block contingency: percentage-of-recovery bans, RFP thresholds and 'paid to find money' optics. The defensible asset is not the model. It is a private labeled dataset of field-test accuracy by meter make, model, size and age matched to its AMI fingerprint. Only a party with no meters to sell can collect it, and each audit adds about 12 ground-truth labels. Recovery is mostly prospective, so the back-billing fight in the parent version never happens.
first_30_days: Pull the 'principal water customers' table from five target utilities' public annual financial reports and the state rate-study calendar. Pick 15 utilities with 10-40k connections and a hearing in the next 9 months. Offer a free 5-business-day screen of the top 100 accounts from one CSV. Line up a test-rig subcontractor and an AWWA-experienced water-loss advisor. Test the top 3 leads at the first free screen for free, using the findings as the proof case. Pre-sell one paid audit with the guarantee to a utility whose hearing is scheduled. Confirm the small-purchase limit in the first two states. Also test the unverified claim that large meters are 40-60% of revenue by checking the annual financial reports.

(2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. title: Mother-Tongue Lifeline for Dementia Flashpoints
one_liner: On-demand live video calls where a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's first language and dialect coaches the English-speaking aide and calms the patient at bath, bedtime and exit-seeking moments.
customer: Home care agencies and PACE programs in immigrant-dense metros (NYC, LA, Miami, Chicago, Bay Area, Houston) with dementia clients whose aides do not share their language. Second: Medicaid managed long-term care and D-SNP plans. Third: families on a flat monthly plan.
problem: Bilingual and multilingual patients lose their second language as dementia advances and drift back to the language, dialect and idioms of their childhood. Agencies send whoever is available. The English-speaking aide cannot say the one calming phrase during the bath, so the bath fails, the patient panics, the aide gets hurt or quits, and the family blames the agency. Telephone interpretation lines translate literally, but a dementia patient's fragments and proverbs need to be validated, not translated. It is a communication problem, not an interpretation problem.
solution: A dedicated line, staffed on demand by trained bilingual retirees, nurses and teachers, covering the long tail: Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Toisanese, Cantonese, Polish, Russian, Uzbek, Punjabi, Tagalog, Greek, Armenian. A tablet or phone is propped where the patient can see it. The specialist speaks to the patient in dialect while coaching the aide in English in the earpiece: 'she's asking for her sister, say she is coming, then hum this song.' Sessions are 3-10 minutes at known flashpoints. Specialists are trained by aides in validation and redirection, not interpretation.
why_now: The post-war Soviet, Chinese, Caribbean and Southeast Asian immigrant cohorts who arrived in the 1960s-80s are now reaching moderate-to-severe dementia. Low-latency video is universal and cheap. AI companions such as KindredMind (voice clone of the caregiver, 12 languages, launched worldwide in May 2026) prove the demand, but they work best for mild cases and comfortable tech users. For moderate-to-severe dementia and live crises, the warm human voice in the right village dialect is the missing complement, and the agencies will pay per minute for it.
revenue_model: $1.25-1.75 per minute billed to agencies and plans, with 60-70 percent gross margin after specialist pay of about $0.45 per minute. Families get $129 per month for 20 sessions. Later, enterprise contracts with MLTC and D-SNP plans that cover the cost as a quality tool.
non_obvious_insight: Patients revert not just to a language but to a specific dialect and era, for example Toisanese, not Mandarin, and the idioms of 1955. A literal interpreter is useless because what calms is tone, a lullaby, a proverb and a familiar name. The buyer is not the family but the agency, which is desperate because language mismatch is why its aides quit its hardest cases. Nobody pays interpreters for companionship, so this talent pool of bilingual retirees is unmined and cheap.
first_30_days: Pick two languages with dense local demand, for example Toisanese or Cantonese in NYC and Haitian Creole in Miami. Recruit 10 bilingual retirees through churches, senior centers and community media. Train them in a one-page validation script. Run it on WhatsApp video with no software. Call 15 small agencies serving those communities and offer 30 free minutes per case. Sign the first three at $1.50 per minute with a $300 monthly minimum.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LanguageLine Solutions, Boostlingo, Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline, KindredMind (AI voice companion for caregiving families). White space: Caveat on confidence: WebSearch hit its session budget (200 of 200) before any of my searches ran. The verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches, not the 6-12 searches requested. I could not run the Crunchbase, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or YC queries. I also could not rule out a small direct competitor: a sub-$5M startup or a local agency-run in-language 'warm line' would not show up in these fetches. Within that limit, I found no product that puts a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's dialect on live video, speaking to the patient and coaching the English-speaking aide at the bedside. The gap is real but narrow. What remains unserved: (1) the crisis-moment human warm voice in long-tail dialects (Toisanese, Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Uzbek and similar) for moderate-to-severe patients; (2) a service sold per minute or per case to home care agencies and PACE programs rather than to families or employers; (3) validation and redirection training for bilingual retirees, where interpreters are trained to translate literally. Interpretation vendors are strong at language coverage and connect speed but have no dementia layer, and nothing stops them adding one. The Alzheimer's Association helpline is a free phone-only substitute. AI companions target mild cases. The main unproven parts are agency willingness to pay $1.25-1.75 per minute, and whether the Medicaid reimbursement structure lets agencies absorb it. At $1.50 per minute, a 6-minute session costs about $9, which is plausible per event, but agencies run on thin margins and no Medicaid code pays for it.

title: Dark Roof Capital: Buy, Cure, Re-Perform
one_liner: Invert the parent. Instead of being paid a $3k fee to cure other people's stranded solar loans, buy those loans at dark-roof prices, finish the systems with a proprietary per-AHJ cure playbook, and keep the full value uplift as a re-performing loan pool.
customer: Sellers: credit unions, banks, servicers and ABS trusts or controlling-class holders that want dark and forbearance-stuck solar loans off their books. Capital side: distressed-credit funds, family offices and NPL buyers who want a new niche but cannot cure a roof. Homeowners are offered a cure and a payment reset in exchange for reinstating payments.
problem: Dark solar loans are an orphan asset class with broken pricing. NPL desks discount them to zero collateral value because they cannot fix the system. Lenders will not cure at scale and cannot collect on a roof that produces nothing. A cure costs perhaps 10-15% of the loan balance yet restores most of its value, but a $3k cure fee captures only about 10% of the $20k+ of value created. The holder of the loan keeps 90%, and today nobody who can cure holds the loan.
solution: Use the forensic pack from the parent as an underwriting engine. Sell a Bid Desk: audit a seller's dark loans, then quote a purchase price within 10 days. First 6 months: sell a zero-upfront cure-share product to a credit union (we finish the jobs, and take about 25% of restored loan value once PTO is achieved and payments resume), funded by a small working-capital line. Then buy pools through an SPV with a licensed sub-servicer. Cure with the playbook and offer borrowers a reset (a rate or principal modification in exchange for reinstatement). Hold or resell re-performing pools. Longer term, securitize re-performing solar loans, as mortgage RPL funds do. Purchases are limited to loans where the borrower is engaged and in forbearance, with reps and warranties and a seller-funded holdback for claims.
why_now: Freedom Forever, Sunnova, SunPower and PosiGen mean a growing pool of dark loans now exists, with forbearance windows expiring. Post-25D, lenders are shifting from origination to workout and want clean books. Mortgage NPL and RPL buyers already exist and are looking for new asset classes in a higher-rate world. Cheap agentic records recovery makes the per-loan diligence cost low enough to bid on small-balance loans.
revenue_model: Phase 1 (0-6 months): cure-share, about 25% of restored loan value, with zero upfront cost to the seller. Phase 2: spread on purchased loans. Illustration only: buy a $35k loan at about $11k (roughly 32% of balance), spend about $3.5k to cure, and a re-performing loan is worth about $24-28k, giving a $10-13k gross uplift before servicing, legal and default haircuts. Investors in the SPV pay roughly a 1.5% management fee and 20% carry above an 8% preferred return. The operating company also earns cure and coordination fees. Phase 3: RPL securitization fees.
non_obvious_insight: Fee-for-service captures the wrong slice of value, and whoever can cure at the lowest cost can bid the highest and still make money. Pure NPL funds cannot cure, lenders will not, and cure contractors have no balance sheet, so the buyer with the best per-AHJ playbook has a structural cost advantage. Dark solar loans also carry a specific hidden liability for buyers. Under the FTC Holder Rule, a homeowner can raise installer misconduct claims against whoever holds the loan. Curing the system removes the basis for most of those claims, so the cure is also the de-risking step, and buyers who cannot cure are pricing that risk at its maximum.
first_30_days: Use the audit engine to build a bid model on 50-100 loans from a friendly credit union or servicer under NDA, and price them. Get a commitment letter from one distressed-credit family office for a $1-2M first-loss pilot. Commission a legal memo on the Holder Rule, state lender and servicer licensing, and rescission risk, and identify a licensed sub-servicer. Sign one cure-share deal (no purchase) covering about 30 loans to measure real cure cost per tier and how many borrowers reinstate. Write a one-page pool teaser for investors. The riskiest assumption is borrower willingness to resume payments and rescission exposure, so measure reinstatement rates before buying anything.

title: Keep-the-Amps: Electrical Carve-Out for Plant Liquidations
one_liner: A 3,000-dollar electrician-verified 'in-place value memo' sold to industrial liquidators, trustees' counsel and corporate closure teams, so the switchgear and transformers are carved out of the equipment auction and sold with the real estate as a powered shell.
customer: Wedge: the 15-30 mid-size Midwest industrial liquidation auctioneers, and the panel trustees, receivers' counsel and corporate-real-estate disposition managers who hire them when a plant with at least 2 MW of service goes dark in OH, PA, MI or IN. Not manufacturers, not brokers.
problem: A plant liquidation has two teams that never talk. The equipment auctioneer sells presses, CNCs and often the switchgear, bus duct and transformers as used-equipment or scrap lots. The real-estate side lists square feet and dock doors. The energized service is the scarce asset (large transformers run about 128 weeks, switchgear 44-90+ weeks, so a buyer who has to replace them loses a year or more), and it is destroyed or stripped in the gap between the two teams. The trustee or seller has a fiduciary or financial duty to maximise proceeds but no document showing what the gear is worth in place versus removed. A secured mortgage lender and an equipment lender may also be fighting over what is a fixture.
solution: Sell one fixed-scope deliverable, the 'Powered-Shell Memo', in 8 days: (1) licensed electrician's one-day walk-through with one-line diagram, nameplates, gear age, thermography and spare capacity; (2) a carve-out schedule marking every item of electrical infrastructure as 'stays with the building' or 'safe to sell', with in-place value (replacement cost plus lead-time cost) against scrap and used-lot value; (3) utility service status (energized, disconnected, minimum-bill exposure) and a one-line check of air and wastewater permit status (shutdown, fees current, notification-only transfer), demoted to a checkbox because Ohio EPA transfer is easy; (4) a buyer-agnostic data-room cut that a data-center, battery, cold-storage or manufacturing buyer can underwrite. The fee is a flat cost line in the auction budget, paid from proceeds at closing, so the estate needs no upfront cash.
why_now: Buyers are paying for existing energized shells (TeraWulf/Anthropic's $19B lease on a shuttered aluminum plant, the former Goodyear plant in Akron running about 150 MW), and transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in years. Plant closures and manufacturer distress continue in 2026, so supply of dead plants is steady. Before the AI-power scramble a stripped switchgear lineup was worth scrap; now it is worth a year of a buyer's schedule.
revenue_model: $3,000 flat per plant (electrician cost about $1,300, analyst about 4 hours, roughly 55% gross margin), paid at closing or as a budgeted line in the liquidation. Add-ons: $1,200 buyer-ready data-room cut, $9,000 for multi-plant corporate closures (3-5 sites), and a $6k-$12k annual retainer for auctioneers who want a standing right to use the memo in their pitches. No percentage of sale price and no brokerage, which avoids the licence problem and the conflict the parent's success fee had. Later: license the anonymised gear-and-value dataset. Bottom-up: 150 to 250 qualifying Midwest industrial disposals a year at $3k-$4k is about $0.5M-$1M of report revenue for one small team before retainers, which is enough to fund the next two offspring-style expansions, not a venture-scale market by itself.
non_obvious_insight: The thing that destroys the power asset in a dead plant is the equipment auction itself, not neglect. The liquidator is paid to turn gear into cash quickly, the real-estate broker never sees the gear list, and nobody owns the question 'is the switchgear worth more bolted to the building?'. The memo is not a report on the building, it is a decision document that changes what goes in the auction catalogue, and it gives the trustee defensible cover for keeping it out.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull 24 months of WARN closure notices for OH/PA/MI/IN, PACER Chapter 7/11 filings by manufacturers with real property, and county receivership dockets, and cross-check against Ohio EPA facility status to list about 60 dark plants with 2 MW or more. Week 2: call 15 regional liquidation auctioneers and 10 trustee counsel with one offer, a free first memo on their next live liquidation in exchange for a written case study and permission to anonymise the data. Weeks 3-4: hire one electrician for two walk-throughs at about $150 per hour; deliver memos; ask one secured mortgage lender to accept a memo as a fixture-line exhibit. Success test: at least one auctioneer pulls electrical gear from a catalogue, and two of the next three mandates pay $3,000 at closing.

title: Megawatt Credit Bureau with Bonded Collateral
one_liner: Invert the vetting desk: real developers pay to be rated, utilities accept the rating for lower deposits, and the company eventually underwrites large-load security bonds off the physical-readiness data, so regulators' collateral rules become the market instead of the threat.
customer: First payer: mid-size and regional developers with real sites and real equipment slots (powered-land developers, ex-bitcoin-miner sites converting to AI, regional colo builders) that are in 10-30 utility queues and being asked for $50K/MW collateral or up to $100K per study in each. Accepting side: co-op and municipal pools that agree to recognize the rating. Capital side: a specialty surety or insurance carrier and reinsurer that provide bond capacity through an MGA structure.
problem: Collateral regimes (Texas proposes $50K/MW, AEP Ohio-style deposits) treat every applicant as a phantom. A real 300 MW project must lock up $15M in cash or letters of credit per utility, and re-submit the same package to each co-op. Hyperscaler-backed developers have the balance sheet and shells do not, so thinly capitalized developers with real projects get squeezed or forced to sell to bigger players. Surety and LC markets price the principal's balance sheet, not the project's physical readiness, so there is no credit signal between a hyperscaler guarantee and a shell LLC. Utilities cannot tell the difference either.
solution: Phase 1 (months 0-6): the 'Verified Ready' dossier for $15-25K. The developer hands over what real projects have (air permit, deed or option, OEM slot confirmation, EPC contract, tenant LOI, financing letter), and the desk verifies it through public records and direct confirmation calls. It issues a dated, registry-anchored readiness rating (R1-R5) that pilot co-op pools accept as satisfying Gates 0-1 and as grounds for a 30-50% deposit reduction or study priority. Utilities pay nothing. Phase 2 (months 6-18): a bonded-collateral program, meaning surety-style 'large-load security bonds' written by a specialty carrier through an MGA, priced off the rating and posted to the utility as obligee in place of part of the cash or LC collateral. Phase 3: publish the methodology as an open standard and lobby tariffs and regulators to reference it, e.g. 'rated applicants may post bonds or reduced collateral.' The registry accumulates milestone-hit data on who actually energizes, which becomes proprietary loss data no one else has.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (final rule due by 12/31/2026), AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs and study fees of up to $100K created a huge new collateral requirement that did not exist 18 months ago, and each dollar of required cash collateral creates demand for a cheaper substitute. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 make equipment evidence a cheap, hard-to-fake readiness signal that a rating can be built on. Roughly half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities and lenders are hunting for a credible signal.
revenue_model: Rating fee $15-25K (up to $75K per GW) per developer per accepting utility set, plus $5K/yr renewals. Bond premium of 2-3% a year on the security amount, with the MGA taking about 20-25% commission plus profit share and the carrier taking the risk. Later, registry data licences to lenders and utilities. Illustrative: 40 rated projects in year 1 is about $800K. At 100 bonded projects a year with $15M average security, that is $1.5B of security, about $37M of premium and about $9M of MGA revenue. It rises further if regulators adopt the rating in tariffs.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators' collateral rules look like the death of a vetting business, but they are the birth of a substitute market, and a substitute needs an underwriter that can price physical readiness. The paying base self-selects to real projects because phantoms will not pay to be scrutinized. The classic conflict of interest of issuer-paid ratings is solved by having the MGA and carrier carry loss exposure, so the rater has skin in the game, unlike a ratings shop. Finally, the segment nobody serves is the thin-balance-sheet developer with real equipment slots, whose risk is legible only in the logistics trail. The rating therefore turns a compliance cost into a moat: loss data on who energizes.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 15 mid-size developers, sourced from the 384 developers on Cleanview's tracker, powered-land brokers and LinkedIn, asking how many co-op queues they are in, how much collateral is posted and how many times they have re-submitted. Days 10-20: pre-sell 3 dossiers at a $10K founding price, refundable if no co-op accepts. Use the free co-op back-test as the lead magnet to sign an MOU with one G&T pool to accept the dossier for deposit relief. Draft methodology v0.1 and publish it openly. Days 20-30: talk to 2 commercial surety brokers or MGAs that already place utility deposit bonds and get term-sheet-level interest, not a binder. Deliver the first dossier. Kill test: if no G&T will trade a rating for lower deposits, the utility-acceptance leg fails and the bond phase never starts.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check. | How this version avoids them: GridUnity and PowerClerk are utility workflow tools, and the rating is a credential they can ingest. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE help developers pick sites or find capacity but do not verify readiness or produce a rating a utility will accept for lower deposits. Cleanview is a public tracker with no verification or credential. ZEG is advisory consulting. NRECA is a distribution channel that can endorse the standard but cannot underwrite. A two-sided credential (developers pay, utilities accept) that later carries insurance-backed loss data has network and data economics none of them touch, and the parent's own problem, that collateral rules substitute for vetting, is turned into the demand driver.

title: Rural Sales Commons: Pay Retiring Appraisers for Comps
one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of retirees paying to leave, pay them for their verified sales books and build the private sales-price registry that non-disclosure states lack, sold first to practicing rural appraisers and later to AVM, lender and assessor buyers.
customer: Supply (paid): retiring and retired certified residential appraisers in roughly a dozen non-disclosure states (for example TX, UT, ID, MT, WY, NM, KS, LA, MS, ND), starting with Texas. Demand: practicing rural appraisers first (subscription), then AVM and hybrid-valuation vendors, rural lenders' collateral-risk teams, county assessors for ratio studies, and eventually programs expanding alternative valuations.
problem: In non-disclosure states, sale prices are not in public deed records. For non-MLS rural sales (FSBO, family transfers, auctions, seller-financed land-with-house), the only record of price is often an appraiser's own phone-confirmation notes and comp files. When the appraiser retires, that sales book is thrown out or dies on a hard drive. Practicing appraisers then struggle to find defensible comps, AVMs and desktop valuations are weakest exactly there (hypothesis to test), and human appraisers stay indispensable and scarce.
solution: Wedge product: a 'Rural Comp Finder' subscription for practicing appraisers in one region, built from a paid capture program. (1) Sales Book Capture: a 2-day white-glove engagement in which we ingest the retiree's comp libraries (a la mode or ClickFORMS exports, spreadsheets, paper binders) with LLM parsing. We keep only transaction facts (date, price, terms, property characteristics, verification source and method), plus the retiree's own adjustment grids and market-area notes. Client and borrower identities never enter the system, and MLS-derived fields are tagged and excluded. The retiree signs a license and certifies what is theirs. (2) Product: county-level search showing each verified sale with provenance (who confirmed, how, when) and a confidence grade, plus a paired-sales adjustment library. (3) Contributor loop: active appraisers who add confirmed sales get a discount, so the commons refreshes after the retirees are gone. (4) Later products: API and data licenses to AVM and hybrid vendors, lenders and county assessors, positioned as ground truth for validating AVMs and alternative valuations.
why_now: About 6-7k appraisers a year are expected to leave (31% of a roughly 65k workforce within 3 years per WorkingRE), and each exit destroys a sales book permanently. UAD 3.6 (mandatory Nov 2, 2026) pushes the industry toward structured data. EO 14393 expands alternative valuations, which need ground truth in thin markets. LLM extraction of messy comp files (old exports, PDFs, handwritten binders) became cheap enough in 2025-26 to make capture affordable.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $39-59 per month per region for active appraisers (contributors pay less). Data licenses of about $25-120k per state per year to AVM and hybrid vendors and lenders, and $15-40k per year to assessors (all unvalidated). Retirees are paid $1,500-3,000 upfront plus a 20-25% royalty pool shared by verified contribution, and that payout is our main cost of goods. Rough plan (assumptions): 20 retirees x about $2,000 is $40k to acquire perhaps 50-100k verified records. 300 subscribers by month 12 is roughly $210k ARR before any data licenses.
non_obvious_insight: The parent asks retirees to pay, but a retiree is a supplier with a ticking clock. Each exit permanently deletes an asset that no later entrant can recreate, and scraping cannot reach it because the value is provenance: who confirmed this price, how and when. First to sign the last generation of phone-confirming appraisers cornered a resource competitors cannot buy once it is gone. Practicing appraisers contributing new confirmed sales gives the commons a network effect that outlasts the retirees. The moat is the counsel-designed data model (provenance tagging, MLS exclusion, client stripping), which turns legal risk into a barrier to fast followers. Because retirees are paid, the parent's unproven willingness-to-pay problem disappears and no earn-out or client transfer is needed.
first_30_days: Gating step: a counsel memo on MLS license terms, the USPAP Confidentiality Rule, GLBA and state board views, and stop or redesign if the extractable data set is too thin. Interview 15 retirees and 15 active appraisers in Texas and ask to see their comp books. Buy 5 sales books at $1,500 as paid pilots, parse them with an LLM pipeline, and tag provenance and MLS-derived rows. Run a blind coverage test on one rural county: how many verified non-MLS sales in the last 5 years the commons holds versus what an active appraiser or an AVM can find. Show the test to 3 AVM or hybrid-valuation vendors and 3 rural lenders and ask for letters of intent. Pre-sell a $39 per month beta to 30 active appraisers. Because the web-search budget ran out, also verify in week 1 whether Cotality, ATTOM or any appraiser comp-sharing group already sells verified non-MLS sales in non-disclosure states.
lineage: mutation of I1039 ('Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors sell data: LIA and OREP sell tail coverage, a la mode stores each user's own files, and Aloft, Valligent, Solidifi, AXIS and PAREA are trainee and supervisor programs, so this idea leaves the trainee, supervisor and client-handoff lane entirely. Aloft, Reggora and AMC-side firms are more likely buyers of the data than competitors. Incumbent data vendors (Cotality, ATTOM, MLS aggregators) depend on MLS feeds and recorder data and would have to buy retiree confirmations one appraiser at a time, which does not fit their scale (unverified, to check in week 1). The design avoids fee-splitting law because no appraisal fee or client revenue is shared, avoids supervisor-licensing issues, and avoids weak client transferability because no clients move.

title: Lender-Paid Calf Collateral Inspection and Lot Grading
one_liner: Sell independent day-3-to-6 lot grading to the feed, milk-replacer and ag-loan credit desks that finance calf raisers, as collateral inspection, so the party who really loses money on every dead calf pays for the measurement.
customer: Credit managers at regional feed and milk-replacer distributors that carry 30-90 day trade credit to calf ranches, and ag lenders and calf-ownership financing programs that lend against calf inventory. Wedge: one distributor with 15-40 non-integrated calf-raiser accounts and $2M or more in calf-related receivables. Raisers are the secondary beneficiary and pay through a loan-document inspection fee or through better credit terms.
problem: A 500-head lot of crossbred calves is now $500-750K of collateral, and the lender's monitoring is still a headcount and the raiser's own say-so. A bad intake lot with poor passive transfer can lose a large share of its calves within weeks (the parent's 10-25% raiser loss is unverified). My inference, to be validated in customer calls, is that the credit desk usually learns of it from a missed payment 30-60 days later. The lender cannot trust the raiser's self-reported Brix, and the raiser cannot prove to the lender that a bad lot was bad luck at intake rather than bad management. Nobody prices the biological quality of the collateral.
solution: For each new lot placed at a financed ranch, an independent tech samples 20 calves within 24-72 hours of arrival (day 3-6 of age), with custody-stamped tube and tag capture. Within 24 hours the credit desk receives a Lot Risk Grade (A-D) built from the Lombard tiers, with an expected 30-day loss band, taken from the published roughly 2x risk for failure of passive transfer at first and replaced by our own pooled data. Credit terms key off the grade: A lots get full limit and fast approval, C/D lots trigger a hold or a risk-sharing plan. The raiser gets a same-day early-warning call for D lots (isolate Poor calves, fluid and treatment protocol), so the inspection is a service to them rather than a tax. Year 2: a loss-outcome dataset licensed to reinsurers and MGAs.
why_now: Crossbred calf collateral per head has multiplied several times over versus a few years ago (beef-on-dairy went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to about 3.2M in 2024 per the parent, and calves have reached $1,500), so headcount-style monitoring that was fine at $100 a calf is negligent at $1,400. Cheap refractometers, phone custody capture and now a published grading standard make lot inspection cost about $1.50-2 a calf. The 2020 consensus tiers give lenders a common language for the first time.
revenue_model: $250-450 per lot inspected (about $1.50-2 per calf), billed to the lender or supplier and recoverable from the raiser as a collateral inspection fee, plus $150-300 a month per financed ranch for the monitoring dashboard. A ranch placing 300 calves a week is about 52 lots a year, or roughly $18K a year. A distributor with 40 accounts is about $700K a year. Later: loss-data license to insurers and reinsurers, and a per-lot fee for a lender-requested claims audit. Market ceiling on fees is modest but recurring, and the buyer's value (bad debt avoided) is a multiple of the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the most money at risk per dead calf is not in the room and is not the raiser. It is the credit provider. Collateral management (independent inspectors working for banks) is an old, boring industry that has never priced the biological quality of livestock. This makes the business independent of two weaknesses in the parent: it needs no buyer premium for graded calves, and it avoids warranty moral hazard because the customer prices and monitors credit rather than insuring loss.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: hold 20 short calls with credit managers at feed and milk-replacer distributors and ag loan officers in one dairy-dense county. Ask what they lose per year to calf-ranch defaults, how they learn of a bad lot, and whether collateral inspection fees are already collectible under their loan documents. Days 15-30: sign a free 60-day pilot with one distributor covering 6 friendly ranches. Two techs, about 12 lots a week, and a 24-hour grade report the credit manager marks up with what they would have changed. At day 60, compare grade against 30-day loss and any past-due behavior, then ask for a signed $300-a-lot agreement. Gate: the credit manager names annual avoided bad debt of at least 10x the annual fee. If lenders will not state a number, kill it. Before pitching, verify the loss-rate and market-size figures and check for existing livestock collateral inspection firms.
lineage: mutation of I0617 ('Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement. | How this version avoids them: Where Food Comes From sells claim verification to marketers, brands and packers. It has no lender product and does no per-lot sampling for credit decisions, so the buyer and the job are different. Calftech-style integrated ranches self-fund and self-monitor, so they are out of scope by design. This targets non-integrated raisers who have to prove intake quality to a lender, and independence is what makes an inspection valid collateral evidence. The $1 self-test objection disappears, because the lender is exactly the party who cannot accept the raiser's own test. There is no dependence on a graded-calf premium (the parent's weakest evidence) and no underwriting exposure. Vets who already test at herd checks work for the raiser and cannot serve as the lender's independent eyes.

title: Aftermarket Support for Stranded DJI Fleets
one_liner: Repair, rebuilt batteries, parts and firmware-independence retrofits for the many legally owned DJI drones that can no longer be replaced with new models.
customer: Police and fire drone units, agricultural spray operators, land surveyors, roofing and solar inspectors, and small public-safety departments with grant money.
problem: The FCC barred new DJI and Autel models in December 2025, US drone tariffs took effect in September 2026 (component tariffs follow in 2027), and China's export controls now cover motors, batteries, radios and sensors. Existing fleets stay legal to fly but face scarce parts and no assured US repair path.
solution: A US repair depot with stocked parts, rebuilt batteries using allied-source cells, gimbal and camera swaps, and open flight-controller retrofits (ArduPilot/PX4) as a migration path. Offer a per-drone maintenance plan with predictive service, and trade-in credits toward US-made airframes, which also become a lead source for those makers.
why_now: The December 2025 FCC action, September 2026 tariffs and export controls all landed within a year. The installed base is large and aging, and no one has a business focused on serving it.
revenue_model: $150-800 per repair, $30-80 per drone per month for maintenance plans, battery and parts sales, and referral fees from US airframe makers on trade-ins.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone debates who replaces DJI, while nobody serves the installed base for the next 5 years. Service earns higher margin than building a competing airframe, starts faster, and gives you the customer list every US-made airframe maker wants.
first_30_days: Buy 20 broken Mavic and Matrice units on secondary markets and set up a bench. Pitch fixed-price maintenance plans to 30 sheriff drone units and agricultural spraying co-ops, and sell the first 10 plans.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
