competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: DJI (own repair, DJI Care, Authorized Service Centers via CarePro Technology Inc), Drone Nerds (plus Drone Nerds Enterprise), Dronefly, BRINC (Safeguard Program). White space: The claim that nobody serves the installed base is wrong. DJI/CarePro, Drone Nerds, Dronefly and small independents already repair DJI drones, and Drone Nerds already sells enterprise hot-swap and always-flying plans. The gap is capacity and guaranteed turnaround. Repair waits reportedly went from days to about three months (https://dronexl.co/2026/09/01/fcc-covered-list-panel-uav-expo-repair-times/), and replacement hardware takes 6-9 weeks. What looks unserved: (1) A US depot with a real SLA (about 72 hours) and loaner pools for Matrice, Mavic 3 Enterprise and Agras spray fleets, sold as overflow capacity to backlogged authorized centers and resellers as well as directly. (2) Agricultural spray operators: DJI has roughly 80% of US spray-drone sales and cumulative tariffs have tripled prices (about $20k to $100k), so these fleets have no affordable replacement (https://dronexl.co/2025/12/17/connecticut-ag-drone-law-tariffs-ban/). FCC docket 26-189 also targets economic-poison spraying drones for retroactive action. (3) Rebuilt batteries from allied-source cells: I found no one doing this at scale, but DJI smart-battery lockouts make it technically uncertain, and I could not check that. (4) Parts stockpiling ahead of the component tariffs that start 2027-02-09. (5) Buying retired fleets from agencies that are switching, for refurbish, resale and parts harvest; El Paso's chief said the department will dispose of its DJI equipment once replacements arrive. The open ArduPilot/PX4 retrofit has no precedent or demand signal that I found. It also does not remove the DJI camera, gimbal and radio modules, so it does not fix compliance. It is the weakest part of the idea.

title: Paid-But-Dark: Solar Loan Book Audit
one_liner: A fixed-fee audit and ongoing watch that tells credit unions, servicers and ABS holders which of their solar loans finance a roof that was never switched on. It then cures the worst ones through a supplier-neutral contractor bench.
customer: Wedge: chief credit or risk officers and loss-mitigation heads at mid-size credit unions and community banks that hold indirect solar loans originated through installer dealer networks. Second wave: servicers and ABS controlling-class investors that inherited books from failed platforms (Solar Servicing LLC-type). Deliberately not the seven Freedom Forever financiers, who already have ops teams and are already staffed. Start with legacy books from Titan, SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, and Mosaic- and Sunlight-financed loans.
problem: Loan tapes track payments, not power. Many dealer-channel programs released milestone money at 'installed', so a loan on a dark roof looks like ordinary credit stress and gets routed to collections, which is the wrong workout. The holder cannot tell installer-caused non-payment from real credit distress. Reserves are mis-sized and nobody in the institution owns the question 'is the system switched on?'. Judges flagged three weaknesses in the parent: the first wave is already staffed, paperwork-only jobs are price-pressured (Atma quotes up to about $1,200), and demand is lumpy.
solution: Step 1, a 10-day Book Audit. Ingest the loan tape (address, funding dates, installer ID, milestone dates). Cross-match it to county permit portals, public state interconnection datasets, borrower-authorized monitoring links and installer status. Output a loan-level tier: Energized, Dark-fixable, Dark-blocked-by-records, or Never-started. Add cost-to-cure, expected recovered loan value, and a one-page loss-reserve summary the CFO can hand to auditors. Step 2, a quarterly PTO-lag surveillance subscription on the whole book and on new originations, with installer-health flags, so nothing goes dark silently again. Step 3, cure orchestration at fixed prices by tier, using an open bench (Atma-type installers, Revival, ECG, Optimus, laid-off crews) and engineering subs. GreenLancer can be a supplier here. The paperwork-only tier is passed through at roughly the $1.2k benchmark plus a fixed coordination fee. The margin lives in the audit, the surveillance and the hard tiers (missing hardware, inspection fixes).
why_now: Freedom Forever went to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026 (claims due Oct 16). It showed that lenders could not see which loans sat on dark roofs, and the same problem is buried in older Titan, SunPower, Sunnova and PosiGen books. The 25D credit ended for 2026 expenditures, so origination volume is down and more installer failures are likely. First-principles cost stack: reading messy permit files and utility portals used to cost $100+ of coordinator time per job. Document and browser agents now do it for a few dollars, so a per-loan audit can be priced below a credit union's discretionary-spend threshold at good margin.
revenue_model: Audit at $10-20 per loan with a $30k minimum (a 3,000-loan book is about $45-60k). Surveillance at $3-6 per loan per year. Cure coordination fee of $300 on paperwork-only jobs. A 20-30% markup on hard-tier cures ($3-8k each). A $500 PTO bonus. Later, licensing of per-AHJ and per-utility playbooks. Bottom-up: 60 institutions in 24 months at about $60k first-year value is about $3.6M before any cure revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The lender's blind spot is a missing column, not missing crews. Selling to the CFO or CRO's loss-reserve problem, instead of to a loss-mitigation desk waiting for the next bankruptcy, turns event-driven demand into continuous demand. Because the audit is a small fixed-fee purchase and not a vendor selection, it slips under procurement thresholds and creates its own list of jobs to cure. A finding of 'this roof is dark' changes the workout from collections to cure, which is where the loan value is recovered.
first_30_days: Week 1: hold 5 calls with credit union CROs and servicer COOs. Ask what they pay today, whether GreenLancer or anyone already covers them, and who owns the reserve question. This is the kill test: if GreenLancer's seven financiers already cover servicers and credit unions, downgrade. Weeks 1-3: build the screen on public data for one state that publishes interconnection records (California's DG Stats is the largest). Publish an anonymized ZIP-level 'permit-final-but-no-PTO' index for Titan and Freedom Forever-era permits as a lead magnet, with no homeowner addresses. Weeks 2-4: offer 3 credit unions a free NDA'd 300-loan scan with a paid full-book option. Recruit 2 ex-installer permit coordinators and sign 2 licensed subs. Goal: one signed paid audit within 60 days.
lineage: mutation of I1175 ('Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GreenLancer (Solar Repair / O&M network), Lender in-house step-in (GoodLeap, Sunrun, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human, Participate, Project Solar; also Dividend Finance), Atma Energy (installer taking over stranded Freedom Forever jobs), Local rescue and completion contractors (Revival Solar, ECG Solar, Optimus Energy Solutions, Advance Solar, Solar Discovery). White space: The unserved wedge is portfolio-level, event-driven triage, not crews. (1) Forensic records recovery at scale. No competitor found sells a forensic pack per stranded loan (AHJ permit file, utility interconnection record, dead installer's CRM and design files, distributor and consignment serials, photo audit) sorted into cure tiers with a cost-to-cure and expected-PTO dashboard across a lender's whole book. GreenLancer and the local rescue firms all work job by job. (2) Servicers, credit unions and ABS trustees without operations. The seven Freedom Forever financiers have ops teams, and Sunrun and GoodLeap have crews. Solar Servicing LLC (which took over Mosaic's servicing), credit unions, bank holders and ABS investors have no step-in playbook. I found no completion vendor aimed at them. (3) Legacy stranded books. Titan (an estimated 150,000 households), SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, Mosaic-financed loans and others. Lenders may not know which loans sit on de-energized systems, so an identify-then-cure offer has little competition. (4) Standby retainer plus pre-negotiated per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer playbooks for the next failure. Not white space: the first-wave Freedom Forever completion work. The stay-relief order dates to about August 2026, so the seven named financiers have probably already picked contractors, and GreenLancer says it already serves seven financiers. | How this version avoids them: GreenLancer sells job-by-job field and engineering work to financiers that already have ops. This sells book-level visibility to holders that have no ops, owns the data layer GreenLancer lacks, and buys GreenLancer-style engineering as a supplier. The seven named lenders and Sunrun/GoodLeap crews keep their in-house step-in, and we do not chase them. We target credit unions, servicers, ABS holders and legacy books. Atma, Revival, ECG and Optimus are the labor bench and not rivals. OhmSnap is homeowner lead-gen and Solar Insure sells warranties to owners after the fact. Enphase's program is post-PTO upsell. None of them sells a lender-side loan-level status product.

title: Yen Gap Audit for Legacy Seven Owners
one_liner: A flat-fee LINE audit that takes HQ's own AI order proposal as the baseline and shows Kansai multi-store Seven-Eleven owners, per item and delivery slot, the yen gap between what HQ suggests and what their own 15/85 contract says they should order.
customer: Owner-operators (individuals or small corporations) running 3 to 10 legacy-contract Seven-Eleven stores in Osaka, Kyoto and Hyogo, who have a contract renewal or a new-store offer within 24 months. Legacy stores are the narrow wedge because Seven's new contract (50/50 disposal share, effective autumn 2027) applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned, so the 15/85 asymmetry persists on existing stores for years. Multi-store owners are the segment that can pay (a 5-store owner pays about 34k yen a month against roughly 4.7M yen of food discarded per store per year), that is most exposed to OFC pressure, and that faces the legacy-versus-new-contract expansion decision. One chain means one contract model. Lawson and FamilyMart wait until their subsidy formulas are verified.
problem: HQ's AI proposes a quantity but never says whose payoff it maximizes. With an 85% owner share of disposal loss, the owner's critical ratio is about 22% (keeps about 24 yen per rice ball sold, loses about 85 yen per one binned) while HQ's is about 70% (earns about 36, loses about 15). Owners cannot audit the proposal and fear the OFC if they deviate. Judges flagged three weaknesses: the asymmetry fades on post-2027 contracts, HQ's markdown push since May 2024 (about 300 items, alerts about 2 hours before expiry) commoditizes a markdown clock, and willingness to pay for software is unproven. Earlier framing as a competing ordering AI also invites a fight with three chains' in-house AI.
solution: Not a better forecaster, a payoff transform. If HQ's recommended quantity approximates the 70th percentile of demand and the owner's optimum is the 22nd, the owner's cut is about 1.3 standard deviations of the slot's demand spread (about 3.9 units for an item averaging 10 with a spread of 3). The tool therefore needs only the HQ proposal (photo of the order terminal screen or printout), the order actually placed, and the store's hourly sales history to estimate the spread. It returns (1) a ranked Yen Gap sheet: the ten biggest expected-yen differences per delivery slot between HQ's proposal and the owner-optimal quantity under that store's own royalty tier and disposal share; (2) an audit of HQ's markdown clock: for the roughly 300 alerted items and for non-alerted items, whether 'two hours before expiry' is earlier or later than the owner-optimal sticker time given the store's sell-through curve; (3) a neutral 'why I ordered differently' one-pager citing expected value under the owner's contract, shown to the OFC only if the owner chooses; (4) a monthly portfolio page with each store's critical ratio and true hourly wage after royalty and own labor, plus an annual memo on whether the next store should be a legacy expansion or a new-contract store. Nothing touches HQ systems.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises 54 yen to 1,231 yen on 1 Oct 2026 and Diamond reported a Seven internal simulation with franchisee profit falling to about one third if wages rise on flat sales. HQ AI ordering is now default at all three chains, so owners follow suggestions they cannot audit. Seven's June 2026 announcement of a new contract with a 50% disposal share concedes the point, and creates a two-tier portfolio (legacy versus new stores) that owners have never had to model. Photo OCR of Japanese printouts and cheap LLM-based structuring make a per-owner concierge audit affordable in 2026, which was not true in 2019.
revenue_model: Entry offer: a paid 30,000 yen '30-day Yen Gap Audit' on one store (credited toward the first 3 months), which tests willingness to pay before any subscription. Then a flat 6,800 yen per store per month (bundle discount at 5+ stores). An annual 150,000 yen next-store-or-renewal decision memo, timed to the moment an owner holds a real 10M-yen decision. Optional 15% gain-share only where a signed baseline exists, so revenue does not depend on disputed savings. Ex-OFC consultants and accountants who refer owners get a 20% revenue share. Bottom-up, if about 5,000 legacy stores sit with 3+ store owners in this segment (an assumption to verify), that is roughly 400M yen a year at full penetration.
non_obvious_insight: The forecast is not the scarce thing, the payoff is. HQ's proposal already encodes a demand distribution, so an owner-side tool can back out the implied quantile and shift it, needing only a spread estimate from the owner's own sales sheets. That makes the product tiny to build and easy to back-test on the founder's three stores. It also flips the political framing: the owner is not overriding HQ's AI, he is applying his own contract to its numbers. Counter-positioning is real, since HQ cannot ship a screen that says its AI is tuned to the wrong payoff without conceding the conflict the JFTC and METI panel already scrutinize.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: back-test on the founder's three stores, comparing HQ proposals against realized sales and disposals, estimating the implied quantile and spread per category, and computing the yen gap. Day 3: one-hour paid review by a franchise lawyer of the confidentiality and third-party data clauses. Days 8-20: sell 10 paid 30,000-yen audits through 3-5 ex-OFC consultants, one or two accountants serving multi-store owners, and Kansai owner LINE and Facebook groups. Kill or pivot signal: fewer than 3 paid at 30,000 yen. Days 21-30: deliver audits, convert the willing to 6,800 yen flat with a 60-day money-back guarantee, and publish a one-page legacy-versus-new-contract critical-ratio table (22% versus about 36%) as owner-to-owner content.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. The unserved wedge is: HQ says X, your own contract math says Y, the yen difference is Z, plus contract-aware multi-store economics. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified. | How this version avoids them: Seven, Lawson and FamilyMart AI ordering and Seven's markdown push are treated as the baseline input, not a rival. The product does not compete on forecast accuracy and audits HQ's markdown clock instead of inventing another. Sinops/Sato and Wasteless/Afresh/Shelf Engine sell to retailers and inherit the retailer's payoff, and none uses a franchisee's contract terms. Too Good To Go is an outlet for surplus, not a decision tool. The Okayama union and ex-OFC consultants give advice without calculators, so they become referral partners rather than substitutes, and the channel does not depend on the small Okayama union. Narrowing to legacy Seven stores avoids the per-chain contract complexity and the shrinking-asymmetry problem of post-2027 new stores.

title: Special-Ed Parent Tracker Feeding Host-School Programs
one_liner: A $20-a-month IEP chief of staff for Texas parents whose service-minute logs identify the families and districts where a clinician-led, voucher-funded host-school program is the real solution.
customer: Texas parents of children with IEPs, reached through special-ed parent groups and pediatric practices, some holding Texas Education Freedom Account (TEFA) funds of about $10K, up to about $30K for IEP students at accredited private schools. Partner: small accredited private schools with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists.
problem: The parent tracker has a low-ARPU, high-CAC consumer business at $20 per month. The host-school program has a high-value payer but no cheap way to find qualified families or to decide where to site a cohort. Parents with documented missed services and a stalled district are stuck, and the money that could fix it is locked behind accreditation and a two-year operating history that they do not have.
solution: Parents upload the IEP and get a legal clock, a service-minute log, records requests and meeting briefs (independent advocates on demand at $75 per 30 minutes). When the log shows sustained missed minutes, the parent sees a clearly labeled 'Plan B' in the app: apply their TEFA funds at a clinician-led program running inside a partner accredited school, where the school is school of record and the operating company supplies the clinical director, staff, curriculum, IEP-style compliance, testing and ESA billing. Firewall: advocate income is flat-fee and never tied to placement, and parents get the compensatory-services claim documented before they leave. First sellable products: the Texas parent subscription plus a January 2027 pilot cohort of 8-10 students at one host school.
why_now: TEFA's first year is underway (2026-27) with $1B in funding and 130,000+ applications in the first three weeks. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students and are closing campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in Oct 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are actively looking for alternatives and an organized paper trail.
revenue_model: Parent subscriptions at $20 per month, advocate sessions at $75 with a revenue split to a vetted co-op, and per-member fees from parent centers and pediatric groups. Host-program management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student (about $6-7.5K per $30K student, $60-75K per 10-student program per year), a 15-20% host-school share, plus a $3-5K design fee per host.
non_obvious_insight: A parent's service-minute log is both a legal claim and a qualified lead: it documents exactly who is failing, in which district, for which disability. Aggregated (with consent), the logs form a district-level heat map that tells the operating company where to place the next host program, because demand is proven in the data. One placed student is worth about 25 years of a $20 subscription in a single year, which pays for the tracker's whole acquisition cost, while the tracker's advocate-first brand makes the placement offer credible rather than salesy.
first_30_days: Publish a free Texas IEP clock calculator and letter templates. With admins of 10 state-level special-ed groups, concierge 30 families and measure violations found. List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin and send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from the 30 concierge families and TEFA parent groups.
lineage: hybrid of I0289 + I1032 (IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents + AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools). Why stronger: The tracker's CAC is subsidized by a payer worth an order of magnitude more per family, and the host program gets pre-qualified, motivated, documented leads instead of buying ads. Shared data tells the business where to open programs. Together it is a full lifecycle (enforce, then exit if enforcement fails) that a competitor with only one half cannot offer.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IEP Advocate.ai, ChatGPT and general LLMs (endorsed by CADRE's parent guide), Parent Training and Information Centers (PTIs/CPRCs), Wrightslaw. White space: Confidence is moderate-low. The WebSearch budget hit 200/200 before I could run the planned 6-12 searches, so I found competitors mostly by fetching guessed and known URLs. More direct competitors probably exist that I did not see, and this should be re-run once the search limit is raised.

The core pitch is NOT white space. Deadline extraction, procedural letter generation, meeting prep briefs and state-complaint drafting are already live at IEP Advocate.ai for $30/mo. Free ChatGPT covers much of the rest. A $20/mo 'AI IEP chief of staff' would be a cheaper copy.

Specific gaps I could not find served in the pages I reached:
1. A service-delivery ledger. This means logging minutes promised vs delivered per IEP service line and turning the shortfall into a compensatory-services claim packet. IEP Advocate.ai's fetched pages do not describe service-minute logging or comp-ed calculation.
2. Human-in-the-loop verification. CADRE and K-12 Dive document AI-drafted complaints with fabricated case law and wrong IDEA readings. A product that combines grounded output with vetted advocate or attorney review, at $75 per 30 minutes, is unserved. IEP Advocate.ai has no human tier.
3. B2B2C distribution through parent centers, disability law clinics, pediatric practices and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month. IEP Advocate.ai lists only individual pricing. The channel is unproven.
4. Evidence-grade record keeping. Time-stamped, tamper-evident logs that a hearing officer will accept, rather than chat history. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Fusion Academy (Nord Anglia), Brightmont Academy, Prenda (microschool platform), KaiPod Learning. White space: Research caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any searches ran, so this verdict rests on about 30 direct page fetches, not the planned 6-12 searches. Google-style discovery of funded startups was not possible, and the negative finding below is unproven. Crunchbase (403), the Comptroller TEFA program pages (404), TEPSAC (503) and several news sites failed.

What the fetches found: no direct competitor was located that runs clinician-led disability programs inside host accredited private schools as the school-of-record structure and bills against TEFA. Adjacent players cover each piece separately.
- Learning-differences schools that build their own campuses: Fusion, Brightmont, Rawson Saunders, Fairhill.
- Microschool platforms: Prenda, KaiPod, Primer.
- Clinician marketplaces: Presence.
- Outside operators embedded in private schools: Catapult.

The unserved wedge is the three-way structure itself. It is a management company that supplies the clinical director, staff, IEP compliance, norm-referenced testing and ESA reconciliation inside a host school. It targets IEP families holding up to $30k accounts in metro Texas in the first TEFA year.

Three risks decide whether the white space is real, and none is resolved:
1. **Legality and accreditor acceptance.** Statute text says a private school must be accredited by a TEPSAC-recognized organization and have continuously operated a campus for at least two school years. It does not address programs within a school or microschools. If the Comptroller, TEA or the accreditor treats a hosted program as a separate campus, or as renting accreditation, the model fails. A 100% pass-through of the ESA to the host with a 20-25% management fee could also draw scrutiny.
2. **Incumbents and hosts.** Existing specialist schools already have eligibility and expertise and may simply expand. Host schools take on IEP compliance liability and reputational risk.
3. **Unit economics.** A 10-student cohort at 20-25% yields $60-75k a year, before clinician cost. Whether that covers a BCBA or dyslexia therapist plus a clinical director was not tested.

title: Private Road Associations in a Box
one_liner: Turn the neighbors' informal, cash-in-a-coffee-can road fund into a recorded, insurable road association with dues, reserves and competitively bid plowing and grading.
customer: Households on private roads and shared driveways (5-60 homes per road). The urgent buyers are the real estate attorneys, title agents and listing agents whose closings stall without an enforceable road maintenance agreement.
problem: Millions of rural households reach their homes by private roads maintained by handshake. One neighbor plows, some chip in, some free-ride. Washouts and disputes are common. Lenders and title insurers often want a recorded, enforceable maintenance agreement, so sales stall. HOA software assumes an incorporated HOA with a manager, not 12 neighbors and a gravel road.
solution: Fixed-fee formation: map who benefits, draft a state-specific maintenance agreement, record it with the county, and set up a simple legal entity or association where state law allows. Then recurring service: ACH dues collection with reminders and lien-based enforcement where allowed, a reserve fund, standing bids from vetted plow, gravel and grading contractors, a photo log of road condition, and storm-damage documentation packages for county or FEMA requests.
why_now: Post-2020 in-migration put many remote workers on rural private roads. Extreme-weather washouts, such as Hurricane Helene's damage to private roads and bridges in western North Carolina in 2024, showed how many neighborhoods have no entity that can pool money or apply for repair aid. Lenders and insurers keep tightening property-access checks. No vertical software serves informal neighbor groups.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 formation fee, paid by the neighborhood or by the seller at closing. $12-25 per household per month for dues administration. A disclosed 5-8% procurement fee on managed contractor bids.
non_obvious_insight: The customer with urgency isn't the neighborhood but the closing. A failed sale costs a seller and an agent five figures, so attorneys and agents will send you deals for a flat fee. Recurring revenue then comes from dues float and admin. At 200 associations you are the largest single buyer of plowing and gravel in a region, which gives you procurement leverage no individual road has.
first_30_days: Pick a state dense with private roads (Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, or the North Carolina mountains). Get an attorney to draft a reusable agreement template. Partner with 3-5 real estate attorneys and title agents who see failed closings. Sell a $1,500 'closing rescue' formation package. Run 2 pilot associations with free dues collection for 6 months to prove the workflow.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:
- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest.

title: Stability Mark: Verified-Stable Tower Registry
one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of screening buildings for sinking, certify the many towers that have been stable for 10-30 years with a satellite-verified public mark and lookup registry that agents, lenders and insurers can trust, later backed by a scoping guarantee.
customer: Wedge: boards and building-specialist listing agents at older concrete towers (1970s-2000s) in Aventura, Sunny Isles, Bal Harbour, Brickell and Miami Beach whose owners are stuck with post-Surfside price discounts and need to prove soundness. Second wave: lenders, title companies, master-policy underwriters and MLS platforms as registry API subscribers. Engineers act as co-signers and reviewers.
problem: After Surfside, buyers, lenders and insurers treat every older tower as suspect until proven otherwise. Milestone and SIRS reports are long, alarming to non-engineers and describe conditions, not movement. Florida condo scores like Domexa's or CondoScan's rest on paperwork (did the board file on time?), not on how the ground and structure have behaved. Fine buildings cannot prove they are fine, and unit owners eat a discount. The parent idea also has a demand flaw: boards do not buy reports that might create a discoverable bad document. Selling fear to a reluctant buyer is hard.
solution: The Stability Mark: a 1-page certificate with a QR code to a live registry page, issued only to towers that pass published, pre-registered criteria. Example criteria: at least 10 years of persistent-scatterer coverage (Sentinel-1 alone gives 2016-2026; ERS/Envisat extend it if Miami coverage is usable), no differential settlement above a stated threshold, no accelerating trend, and a matched-control comparison. Participation is opt-in. Passing towers are published. Ambiguous or failing towers get a private result and a monitoring plan, with no public listing. The certificate covers the measurement, not structural safety, and a PE co-signs the method. The method is open and reproducible. There is annual re-verification with automatic revocation triggers, MLS-compatible listing fields, and a lender and insurer API. In year two, add a Scoping Guarantee: a reinsured parametric cover that pays for the Phase 1 engineering evaluation ($15-40K) if a certified tower later trips the threshold, priced at about $150/building/year. The certifier's own capital then stands behind the mark.
why_now: Post-Surfside stigma on older Florida towers is still discounting resale values, and inventory has been elevated since 2024-25 (verify current data). The Dec 31, 2026 milestone deadlines are about to push a wave of alarming paperwork at buyers who cannot interpret it. Reserves can no longer be waived from 2026, so buyers ask about condition. Only satellite archives hold a 1990s-to-present record of how a tower behaved: FIU found Champlain Towers South's 1990s subsidence in ERS data, and no sensor bought today can create that history. Free Sentinel-1 and OPERA data plus NISAR (L-band, from June 2026) make re-verification cheap. Estructura's fear-first marketing leaves the good-news position empty.
revenue_model: Initial certificate $1,800 per building ($995 founding price for the first 50), then $500/year re-verification. PE review fee of about $250 per certificate, and about $60-100 of compute per building. Year two: registry API for lenders, title and insurers at $20K/year flat or $1-3 per lookup, and Scoping Guarantee premium of about $150 per building per year. Year one: about 150 marks at about $1,400 average is roughly $210K, plus $75K recurring. The 10x case: several thousand concrete towers in Florida and tens of thousands nationwide (assumed, verify), with Gulf, Houston, Tampa, Jersey City and Honolulu next. A registry adopted by MLS platforms and lenders, plus a warranty book, is a platform business that a report shop cannot become.
non_obvious_insight: Mandatory-inspection regimes create fear purchases. A voluntary mark creates status purchases, and it has an unraveling dynamic: once 20-30% of comparable towers in a submarket carry the mark, silence becomes a signal that a building is sinking or hiding something, so competitors' badges drive demand rather than the board's fear. Demand rises non-linearly with adoption, which no report business gets. The 10-30 year archive is a cornered resource: nobody can retroactively install a 1996 sensor. Every engineer-reviewed pass or fail adds to a proprietary labeled dataset of which radar signatures precede real findings, which tightens the thresholds and beats sensor bundles that only see the future. The warranty forces honest calibration, since the certifier pays if it is wrong.
first_30_days: Take the parent's roughly 400-tower Sentinel-1 stack and process the 150 oldest concrete towers against the full available archive. Publish the pass criteria before running the results. Confirm persistent-scatterer density and ERS/Envisat usability on Miami; if pre-2015 coverage is poor, use the Sentinel-1 decade. Contract one PE or geodesist to co-sign a methodology memo with measurement-only wording. Approach 10 building-specialist listing agents and 10 presidents of towers that passed, at the $995 founding price. Aim for 8 marks sold, 3 live on agent sites or MLS remarks with the QR code, and 2 lenders or title underwriters willing to read the registry page. Kill test: if fewer than 5 of 20 boards buy at $995, or no PE will co-sign the wording, stop.
lineage: mutation of I1289 ('Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Estructura (division of Dorado Services) - TerraIntel InSAR + GeoSIG sensors + GeoSMART, TRE ALTAMIRA (CLS Group; TRE Altamira Inc.), Sixense Satellite / Atlas InSAR (Vinci group), Fugro (InSAR high-rise settlement evaluation and prediction). White space: No one found sells a productized, fixed-price, board-readable per-building InSAR settlement history for Florida condo towers, wholesaled to the engineers who already write milestone and SIRS reports. The InSAR firms (TRE Altamira, Sixense, Fugro, SkyGeo, Detektia) sell quote-based enterprise projects. SatSense does per-property InSAR but for the UK. Estructura (June 2026) pitches InSAR to condos but only as one part of a sensor bundle, with no disclosed price and no report artifact. The Florida condo-data players (Domexa, CondoScan, CleanCondo, PropFusion) have no physical-movement data. Specifically unserved: (1) a $400-$2,500 report an engineer can attach to a Phase 1 milestone inspection or SIRS; (2) a 10-30 year ERS/Envisat/Sentinel-1 history that shows a building is stable, for lenders and underwriters; (3) a pre-construction baseline for a neighbouring tower's pile driving; (4) a roll-up for management companies with many buildings. A strong caveat is that this is not a technology moat. TRE Altamira already processed this exact coastline, ISCE, MintPy and StaMPS are open source, and OPERA gives a free coarse baseline. Any incumbent or Estructura could productize this quickly, so the wedge is distribution through engineers, engineer sign-off, and price. | How this version avoids them: Estructura, SmartCore, TRE Altamira, Fugro, Sixense and the other InSAR shops all sell risk detection and monitoring, which is a fear purchase, and none offers a public verified-stable credential. Estructura is also counter-positioned against it: its sensor and AI subscription depends on unseen risk, and a satellite all-clear would cannibalize it, so it cannot rationally copy the mark. Domexa, CondoScan and CleanCondo are paperwork-based scores, paid by buyers at thin price points ($49). The Stability Mark supplies the physical-behavior layer they lack, so Domexa is a distribution partner (they could embed the mark in their scores). OPERA is free but coarse and carries no attestation or per-building certificate. SatSense and Detektia target insurers and engineers abroad. The moat is a published standard, a PE panel, MLS and lender adoption, a labeled dataset and guarantee capital. A copycat has to rebuild all of it.

title: ERCOT Large-Load Energization Files, Fixed Fee
one_liner: A two-engineer Texas specialist that sells neocloud and colo developers a fixed-fee, six-week package of ISO-acceptable PSS/E and EMT models, a ride-through study and a compliance file, with a fee kicker paid when ERCOT accepts it.
customer: Wedge: VPs of power and interconnection leads at 30-60 mid-size neocloud, colo and AI-campus developers with 25-300 MW sites in ERCOT's large-load study queue, plus the EPCs that own their energization schedule. They have no in-house power-electronics staff. Hyperscalers with in-house power simulators are excluded on purpose.
problem: Since PGRR115 and NPRR1234 (effective late 2025), ERCOT wants studies and dynamic models for loads of 25 MW or more before energization. NOGRR282 (effective Aug 1, 2026) adds frequency and voltage ride-through requirements for large computational loads. A developer holds only OEM spec sheets. UPS and power-shelf control details sit behind OEM NDAs, and bespoke PSCAD consultants are slow and have never modeled a GPU power shelf. Every rejected model or resubmittal loop delays energization. At 100 MW of leased AI capacity, a month of slip defers roughly eight figures of rent or GPU revenue (rough estimate: about $100+/kW-month of critical IT), so a $150k package is a rounding error next to the delay it prevents.
solution:
Sell acceptance, not artifacts, in four steps.
1) A $15-25k gap analysis against the NOGRR282, PGRR115 and NPRR1234 texts, using the site's one-line diagram and UPS/PSU bill of materials.
2) A fixed-fee package of $90-180k: an ISO-submittable PSS/E dynamic model and EMT model, a ride-through and oscillation study, and a compliance file. It is built from reusable platform-level models of specific UPS, power-shelf and facility archetypes. Those models are HIL-validated at a partner lab (Typhoon HIL or OPAL-RT time, or a university lab) under OEM NDAs.
3) Submission handling and resubmittal support through ERCOT's large-load process.
4) A 25% success kicker paid on ERCOT acceptance, plus an annual re-issue subscription when GPU generation, UPS firmware or 800V DC changes the load.
why_now: NOGRR282 was approved July 9, 2026 and took effect Aug 1, 2026. PGRR115 (Nov and Dec 2025) and NPRR1234 (Dec 15, 2025) already gate energization on studies and models. The first wave of 25 MW and larger neocloud sites is hitting the queue now, before any consultancy has a large-load specialty. Rubin-generation hardware and 800V DC change the load behavior again within 12-18 months, which creates re-issue demand.
revenue_model: $15-25k gap analysis, $90-180k fixed-fee package, and a 25% success kicker on acceptance (about $25-45k). Add $20-40k per year model maintenance and re-issue per site, and later OEM test-and-listing fees for platform models. A year-1 target of about 12 packages at about $150k is roughly $1.8M with 2-3 engineers. Reuse of platform models across sites is what lifts gross margin past a consultancy's 30-40%.
non_obvious_insight: The developer does not want a model. It wants ERCOT's planners to sign off without a resubmittal loop. The durable business in inverter modeling after Blue Cut was not the model libraries, because vendors and ISOs published those. It was the shops that knew what the ISO's planners would accept. A single-regulator focus (ERCOT only) lets a two-person shop become the known acceptance expert in six months, and each accepted submission is precedent no generalist consultant has. Free generic EPRI or NERC models help us: they are conservative, and a developer who submits them risks being told to add buffer capacity or accept curtailment, while a product-specific validated model avoids that.
first_30_days: Week 1: read the actual NOGRR282 protocol text ('Large Electronic Load Ride-Through Requirements', 282NOGRR-01) and the PGRR115 and NPRR1234 submission forms. Call ERCOT large-load working group and planning contacts to confirm what compliance evidence is required. If it is self-attestation only, price down to gap analysis plus study and keep the acceptance-kicker idea for models only. Weeks 1-2: recruit one ex-ERCOT or TO planning engineer (Texas PE) and one power-electronics engineer, and publish an open ERCOT LCL Readiness Checklist. Weeks 2-4: work the public ERCOT large-load queue reports to list about 40 developers and the 10 biggest EPCs, and sell three $15k gap analyses. Sign a lab MOU and get a first UPS or power-shelf OEM NDA through the first paying customer's equipment.
lineage: mutation of I0996 ('Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Typhoon HIL (Data Centers solution), OPAL-RT (HYPERSIM, power-HIL), EPRI DCFlex, Emerald AI (Emerald Conductor). White space: Across this session's research I found no direct competitor selling packaged, hardware-validated large-load dynamic models (PSS/E plus EMT) with ride-through study reports and certification letters for GPU-cluster, PSU and UPS stacks. Nobody was seen selling OEM-level type-test certification for power shelves and UPS platforms. Adjacent players cover only pieces: HIL tools (Typhoon HIL, OPAL-RT), generic EMT consultancies, EPRI's flexibility consortium, workload-flex software (Emerald AI), and simulation software vendors with no data center library shown.

Three structural threats need answers:
1. Regulators and EPRI or NERC may publish free generic composite or EMT models, which commoditizes the model library.
2. OEMs (UPS, PSU, NVIDIA) own the confidential control details and may ship their own models.
3. Per-project EMT consulting already exists and is not verified either way for large loads.

The defensible white space is independent, hardware-validated, ISO-acceptable model packages and compliance evidence for the 25-500 MW neocloud and colo developers who lack in-house power simulators. It would be reused across sites through OEM platform type tests, not sold as bespoke studies.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before this task began, so competitor discovery relied on direct page fetches and GitHub search. Startup databases (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt), news, and NERC or EPRI publication pages were not checked. Several NERC, EPRI and PJM URLs returned 404 or empty content. Treat the 'no direct competitor' finding as moderate-confidence. Verify manually against NERC LLTF outputs, EPRI data center model reports, and WECC or ERCOT model requirements before committing. | How this version avoids them: Typhoon HIL and OPAL-RT are tool vendors, so we partner and buy their HIL time and they act as a channel. Electranix and Danovo do bespoke per-project studies for generators and transmission owners with no reusable GPU or UPS platform models and no ERCOT large-load precedent, and they are slower and costlier per site. EPRI DCFlex and free generic models are baselines we start from, not substitutes, because ERCOT wants site-specific and product-specific evidence. Emerald AI sells workload flexibility, whereas we sell compliance evidence for the fixed, fast-ramping load. Pearl Street speeds steady-state generation studies and has no dynamic large-load work. Hyperscaler in-house simulators are avoided by targeting only developers without them. Siemens PSS/E is the file format we deliver into, not a competitor.

title: Refund-Netted Dating: Wholesalers Fund the Float
one_liner: Sell regional wholesalers and buying groups a claim-underwritten '28-day MFP dating' program that defers payment on MFP-drug invoice lines and nets them against the refund, so the pharmacy never borrows and the wholesaler is paid a dilution-risk fee to us.
customer: The independent-pharmacy channel head or CFO at regional full-line wholesalers, independent buying groups and non-wholesaler-owned PSAOs. These are the first wave because they can decide in weeks and cannot out-finance the Big 3 on other terms. The franchise programs of the Big 3 (Good Neighbor Pharmacy, Health Mart, Leader) come second. The pharmacy is the beneficiary, not the payer of record.
problem: The wholesaler owns the weekly auto-debit, the invoice detail and, as a possible third-party support entity, a view into refund flows. It is the cheapest and best-placed capital in the system. But the float squeezes its customers. NCPA-cited behavior includes 70% of pharmacies limiting stock of high-cost drugs and 60% using personal or business savings. That means lost brand volume, rising credit exposure to weakened accounts, and closures (SCPC warns 60% of its members may close). Wholesalers have not extended MFP dating at scale because they see invoices, not claims. They cannot tell which MFP refunds are safe or price the dilution risk of reversals, disputes and 340B rejections. Outside lenders sit behind the wholesaler's debit and cannot fix this.
solution: 'MFP Dating Desk' is software plus a capped dilution guarantee. 1) Connect the wholesaler's invoice and EDI feed with each participating pharmacy's PMS claims export and MTF remittance files, with the pharmacy's consent given inside the wholesaler's normal account flow. 2) Each week, match MFP-drug invoice lines to eligible claims and score dilution risk. 3) The wholesaler moves those lines into a 28-day bucket, or nets them against the refund where it already handles payment routing. 4) We cover dilution losses above the pharmacy's holdback, up to a cap, funded by our reserve and excess capacity from a credit fund or licensed carrier. The guarantee is structured as contractual recourse or through a licensed carrier so it is not unlicensed insurance. 5) The pharmacy sees one dashboard showing what is deferred and when the refund clears. Extended trade terms are commercial credit, not a loan, which avoids most of the lending-license and disclosure work in offspring one.
why_now: In January 2026 the refund lag became a recurring weekly mismatch between 14-day wholesaler terms and a 21-day refund average. On January 1, 2027 semaglutide and 14 other drugs join and the mismatch grows. Independents are choosing wholesalers and buying groups for 2027 terms, so a cash-flow feature is a retention weapon. CMS now expects manufacturers to include cash-flow mitigation in their refund plans, which shows the problem is recognized but unsolved on the distribution side.
revenue_model: The wholesaler pays a platform fee of about $5k a month plus about $10 per active pharmacy, and a risk-and-data fee of about 0.25-0.5% of the deferred refund amount per cycle, calibrated to measured dilution. The wholesaler recovers this through a small service fee. The pharmacy's all-in cost lands near 8-12% annualized, in line with bank A/R lines and well below an MCA. Illustrative: a regional wholesaler with 300 senior-heavy accounts averaging $50k of float has $15M deferred at any time. That is roughly $0.4-0.9M a year of risk fee before losses. Add more wholesalers and buying groups without adding a lending license.
non_obvious_insight: The parent treated the wholesaler as an obstacle. It is actually the best-collateralized lender in the chain, because it holds the debit right, the invoice line item and the relationship. It does not lack capital. It lacks a price for statutory-refund dilution, and that price lives in claim-level data it does not own. Selling underwriting to the party that owns the rails turns a capital-intensive 15-25% lending business into a small fee on a much larger base. It also removes the CAC problem, because the wholesaler's sales reps are the distribution.
first_30_days: List 15 regional wholesalers, buying groups and independent PSAOs and reach the CFO or independent-channel head through association conventions and cold outreach. The pitch is a free 'MFP exposure map' built from their own invoices. Aim for one 60-day shadow pilot with no cash at risk, covering 20-30 senior-heavy accounts. Compare what the deferral would have cost against measured dilution, and use it to set the fee. In parallel, get indicative excess-of-loss terms from one credit fund or specialty carrier and check with counsel whether the guarantee needs a license.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: Reconciliation vendors (SpendMend, Plenful, ScriptPro, Liberty, Beacon) sell to the pharmacy or health system and end at a report. We sell to the wholesaler and end at a credit decision, so we are not in their category. The Big 3 are listed as adjacent competitors that own the rails. Here they are the eventual channel, not a rival. They can build it but are slow, and the regionals cannot build it at all. No pharmacy borrows, so there is no 15-25% versus 8-12% pricing fight with Live Oak, Corporate Capital Direct, ARF or other lenders, and no borrowing-base conflict with the pharmacy's bank. Wholesaler payment priority is the design, not a risk. The main risk is a Big 3 in-house build. The defenses are speed in the regional segment and a licensable neutral data layer.

title: One Binder Scan: Lender Monitoring Plus Warranty Recovery
one_liner: One AI read of a data hall's closeout binders yields both a lender's ready-for-service probability and an owner's serial-level warranty ledger, with contingency warranty recovery as the reason the owner grants access.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and insurers lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts (pay a fixed monitoring fee). Colo developers, powered-shell landlords and neocloud owners with energized but idle halls (pay a share of recovered warranty value).
problem: Lenders need interior truth about the last 90 days before ready-for-service but borrowers resist giving data-room access to a monitor. Owners of energized-but-empty halls don't know their OEM warranty clocks are silently running out. Both parties need the same documents (gear serials, startup sheets, Cx reports, integrated test results, punch lists) and neither has staff to read them.
solution: An LLM pipeline ingests POs, bills of lading, startup sheets, Cx sign-offs and maintenance logs into one serial-level ledger. Lender view: a Readiness Ladder score with probability of ready-for-service by date, covenant and draw triggers, and OEM startup-tech calendar risk. Owner view: warranty expiry dates, voiding conditions, and a hit list of claims and start-date deferrals to file within 90-120 days. Sold as a $25K two-week lender second opinion, made economical by a contingency warranty scan (25-30% of recoveries) offered free to the owner. Structure the two views as separate teams with an information wall, and route recoveries through the lender-controlled operating account so the independence of the monitor is not compromised.
why_now: About half of 2026 US capacity is slipping and neocloud credit is a live worry, so lenders are capping exposure. Many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak, tariff-inflated prices, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. Satellites have commoditized the exterior, leaving the interior (binders and commissioning data) as the scarce truth. LLMs now read messy closeout binders cheaply.
revenue_model: Lender side: $25K two-week second opinions, $40-120K full pre-close diligence, $8-20K per month per facility monitoring. Owner side: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and deferrals, $150-400 per asset per year tracking, $15-40K closeout audits, and PO-stage clause packs that defer warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty ledger and the readiness score are built from the same binder, so the second product costs almost nothing to produce. The biggest barrier to interior monitoring is borrower cooperation, and a free contingency service that recovers money is the best incentive to provide it. Expiring warranties and unavailable OEM startup techs are also leading indicators of delay, so each product improves the other's signal. The lender's covenant becomes the distribution channel to owners at the moment they have binders and idle halls. Ethyco offers warranty-phase support but not idle-hall contingency or lender integration.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Find 3 owner-operators through Cx and PM networks whose halls energized 8-11 months ago and are not fully loaded, and offer a free 10-day binder scan on contingency. Build the extraction on real binders (gensets, UPS and chillers first) and deliver an 'expiring in 90 days' hit list. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and pitch 5-10 private credit desks a $25K two-week second opinion on one live deal, using the scan as proof of depth.
lineage: hybrid of I0365 + I0229 (Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders + Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls). Why stronger: Double revenue from one document-processing pipeline, with two payers whose interests line up. Owners get paid to be monitored, lenders get better collateral and cleaner data, and access friction disappears. A serial-number equipment register across financed halls becomes a data moat that single-purpose competitors (satellite monitors or Cx firms) cannot replicate.
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline.

title: Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes
one_liner: A micro-bounty network that pays home inspectors, plumbers and water-heater installers to photograph where the service line enters the basement, with AI classification, so utilities can clear 'unknown material' lines for about $40 each instead of $500-3,000 each.
customer: Mid-size municipal and district water utilities (20k-300k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their published lead service line inventory. The buyer is the utility director or the lead program manager. A secondary payer is the home buyer, who pays about $29 for a 'Lead Line Certificate' add-on at inspection.
problem: Since the lead and copper inventory requirement, every system has had to classify each service line as lead, galvanized-requiring-replacement, non-lead or unknown. Unknowns are a legal and financial liability, and they are hard to shrink. The only sure verification is potholing or excavation, which costs hundreds to thousands of dollars per line. Customer self-ID by mailer gets a response rate of roughly 10-25%. Absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. Utility crews can't look inside private basements, so tens of thousands of unknowns sit in the spreadsheet for years.
solution: A mobile app with a fixed 3-photo protocol: the pipe where it enters the building, a scratch or magnet test close-up, and the meter serial number with the address. A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, PEX, PVC or HDPE, or flags it as unresolved. Humans QA the low-confidence cases. Each submission is geo-verified and tamper-evident, and exports in the format the state inventory portal expects. Inspectors and plumbers earn $15-25 per verified line, and the platform earns the spread. The utility gets a reconciled inventory feed and a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP code. The consumer add-on (inspector-branded certificate, sold to the buyer) pays the inspector while giving the utility free data.
why_now: The first inventories were filed in late 2024, and public analyses showed millions of lines still classified 'unknown'. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements set a 10-year replacement clock that starts around 2027, though federal details keep being revisited and litigated. Several states have their own replacement statutes that don't depend on the federal rule. The $15B in dedicated infrastructure-law lead line money is moving through state revolving funds under spend-down pressure. Vision models are only now accurate enough to classify pipe photos. (Regulatory details are from memory. Verify state acceptance rules before pitching.)
revenue_model: Utilities pay $30-60 per verified line, sold as a per-line contract that fits under small-purchase thresholds. A $10-25k pilot is typical, followed by annual contracts. The consumer-paid certificate ($29) is split with the inspector. Later products are inventory-reconciliation SaaS and an access-agreement workflow for replacement crews.
non_obvious_insight: Utilities think they have a data problem, but they have an eyeballs-in-basements problem. Every home sale (an inspector visits) and every water heater swap (a plumber stands three feet from the service entry) already puts a paid expert next to the exact pipe that matters. Nobody has paid them for a photo yet. Excavation is the wrong tool for a question that visual inspection answers for almost nothing.
first_30_days: Pick one state that accepts documented visual or contractor verification. Pick two utilities in it whose public inventories are more than 40% unknown. Recruit 30 inspectors through local InterNACHI and ASHI chapter meetups and Facebook groups, and pay a launch bonus per photo set. Run a 200-line pilot. Have the utility pothole 30 of those lines as ground truth, then publish the accuracy numbers. Close a $15-25k pilot purchase order with the first utility, using the small-purchase limit that many cities set at $25-50k so no council vote is needed.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply.
